K-273.h1: Number Bonds to 5: The First Part-Part-Whole Page
K-273.title: Number Bonds to 5 for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-273.metaDescription: Number bonds to 5 worksheet: six part-part-whole bonds with counting dots in the whole. Write the missing part in the dashed circle. Free kindergarten PDF.
K-273.p1: Every bond on this Kindergarten worksheet has the same whole: 5. Six part-part-whole diagrams fill the page, each one a large whole circle joined to two smaller part circles, and beneath the numeral in the whole circle runs a row of five counting dots. One part is printed; the other is a dashed, empty circle. The child counts the dots, sees how many of them the printed part already accounts for, and writes the number that finishes five.
K-273.p2: Five is the right whole for a first bond page because it can still be held in the hand and taken in at a glance. A child who cannot yet recall that 3 and 2 make 5 is not stuck here: they count the dots, cover the printed part with a finger, and count what is left, so the picture does the teaching while the number knowledge catches up. That bridge from counting to knowing is the entire purpose of the dots. It is also why five comes before ten — there are only two pairs to meet, they come round again and again, and most children start finishing the bonds from memory within a page or two.
K-273.p3: Print the PDF free and let the counting happen out loud; it fades on its own once the pairs are known. When the bonds of five arrive without a pause, number bonds within 10 widens the range one whole at a time, and the make ten page brings the dots back for the pairs every first grader eventually needs by heart.

K-274.h1: Number Bonds Within 10: A Different Whole Every Time
K-274.title: Number Bonds Within 10 for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-274.metaDescription: Number bonds within 10 worksheet: six bonds with wholes from 5 to 10 and no counting dots. Write the missing part in the dashed circle. Free kindergarten PDF.
K-274.p1: The six bonds on this Kindergarten page do not share a whole. One card asks about 7, the next about 9, the next about 5 — any whole from 5 to 10 can turn up, and there are no counting dots to lean on this time. Each bond prints the whole and one of its parts, and the child writes the missing part into the dashed circle. Six bonds, six fresh starts, no two the same.
K-274.p2: Mixing the wholes is a deliberately awkward choice, and that is exactly where its value lies. On a single-whole page a child can answer the second card without really reading it, because the number at the top never changes; here the first thing to check is which whole this particular bond is about. Teachers spot the tell immediately — a child who writes a partner for 10 on a card whose whole is 8 has been running on autopilot rather than reading. A mixed page catches that habit early, while it is still cheap to fix, and it pushes the child toward genuinely holding several different decompositions at once instead of one rehearsed set.
K-274.p3: The sheet prints free as a PDF and takes only a few minutes. It follows naturally after number bonds to 5, where the dots still do some of the work, and once these feel comfortable, number bonds to 20 carries the very same picture past the ten barrier.

K-275.h1: Number Bonds to 20: Part-Part-Whole Past Ten
K-275.title: Number Bonds to 20 for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-275.metaDescription: Number bonds to 20 worksheet: six part-part-whole bonds that all make twenty. Write the missing part in the dashed circle. Free printable kindergarten PDF.
K-275.p1: Every one of the six bonds on this page has 20 sitting in the whole circle. The diagram is unchanged — one whole joined to two parts, one of them dashed and empty — but the numbers are bigger: the child reads 20 and a part such as 13, and has to work out the partner that completes twenty. There are no counting dots and no counters printed anywhere, just the bond and the thinking that fills it.
K-275.p2: Bonds of twenty are where the picture starts earning its keep as a strategy tool rather than a puzzle. Most children solve them by leaning on what they already know about ten: twenty is ten and ten, thirteen uses one ten and three more, so seven are left. Watching which route a child takes is genuinely informative — counting on by ones from thirteen says the ten structure has not landed yet, while an answer that arrives whole says it has. Either way, the pairs that make twenty are the facts sitting underneath two-digit addition a year or two later.
K-275.p3: Print it free as a PDF and ask how each answer was found; the method matters more here than the six numbers do. Children who wobble can drop back to number bonds within 10 for a page, and those who fly through are ready for mental math within 20, where the same pairs reappear stripped of their circles.

K-276.h1: Number Bonds: Find the Missing Whole
K-276.title: Number Bonds: Find the Whole | Free Printable PDF
K-276.metaDescription: Number bonds worksheet with the whole missing: both parts are printed and the child writes the total in the dashed top circle. Free printable kindergarten PDF.
K-276.p1: This Kindergarten number bonds worksheet turns the usual task around. On all six bonds the two parts are printed and the big circle at the top — the whole — is the dashed, empty one. The child reads the two parts, puts them together, and writes the total into the whole. The answers run from 6 to 10, so the numbers stay friendly while the direction of the thinking quietly flips.
K-276.p2: Reversing the blank changes the operation without changing the picture. Finding a missing part is subtraction wearing a friendly diagram; finding the missing whole is plain addition — and children who have only ever seen one of the two often assume that every bond means take away. Working both directions on the same shape is what makes the part-whole relationship flexible rather than a memorized procedure, and it is the same insight that fact families formalize a year later. Expect a few children to subtract out of habit on the first card. One question usually settles it for good: are we putting these together, or breaking something apart?
K-276.p3: The page prints free as a PDF and pairs beautifully with number bonds within 10, which keeps the blank down in a part, so a child can meet both directions in a single sitting. After that, fact families to 10 gives the same three numbers a house of their own to live in.

K-277.h1: Make Ten: Number Bonds with Counting Dots
K-277.title: Make Ten Number Bonds with Dots | Free Printable PDF
K-277.metaDescription: Make ten worksheet: four large number bonds of 10 with counting dots in the whole. Write the missing part in the dashed circle. Free printable kindergarten PDF.
K-277.p1: Four large number bonds fill this Kindergarten page, and every one of them makes ten. Beneath the numeral in the whole circle runs a row of ten counting dots; one part is printed and the other waits as a dashed circle. Because there are only four bonds and each is drawn big, the page is unhurried — the child counts the dots, reads the part that is given, and writes the partner that completes ten.
K-277.p2: Four large cards instead of a dense grid is a classroom decision as much as a design one. A page like this works on a table between two children, under a document camera, or in a small pull-out group where every dot has to be visible from across the table — and the dots give the group something concrete to point at while they argue their way to an answer. The pairs that make ten deserve that much attention, because they are the facts behind bridging strategies, mental addition, and eventually every column method the child will ever meet.
K-277.p3: Print the PDF free and keep a copy for the group table. Children who need a smaller whole first can start with number bonds to 5, where the dots do the same job at half the size, and once ten is secure, number bonds to 20 is the natural step up.

G1-214.h1: Mental Math Within 10: Twelve Quick Facts
G1-214.title: Mental Math Within 10 for Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-214.metaDescription: Mental math within 10 worksheet: twelve mixed addition and subtraction facts to solve in the head, one answer box each. Free printable Grade 1 PDF.
G1-214.p1: Twelve bare number sentences sit in a tidy grid on this Grade 1 page, and every one of them stays within 10 — some add, some subtract, all of them answered in the head. There is nothing to decode: no pictures, no story, no space for working. The child reads a fact, thinks, and writes the answer in the box at the end. Plus-one and minus-one facts are kept off the page on purpose, so all twelve are worth solving, and the whole sheet takes two or three minutes.
G1-214.p2: Within 10 is the band where fluency has to be built first, because everything above it borrows from here. A child who still counts on fingers for 7 minus 3 will count on fingers for 17 minus 3 as well, and later for 47 minus 3, spending on retrieval the attention that the real problem needs. Keeping the numbers small makes the actual goal visible: not correctness, which most first graders can reach eventually by counting, but speed and calm. That is why a short page done often beats a long page done once.
G1-214.p3: The worksheet prints free as a PDF and makes an ideal daily warm-up. Children whose facts are still fragile can rebuild them on number bonds to 10, where the same pairs appear as a picture, and once ten feels easy, mental math within 20 raises the ceiling without changing the routine at all.

G1-215.title: Missing Number Equations to 20 | Free Printable PDF
G1-215.metaDescription: Missing number equations to 20 worksheet: twelve problems where the box moves to the front, middle or end. Solve mentally. Free printable Grade 1 PDF.
G1-215.p1: Twelve equations within 20 fill this Grade 1 page, and the empty box moves around. On some cards it sits where you would expect, after the equals sign; on others it stands at the front or in the middle, so the child meets sentences shaped like a box plus 3 equals 8, or 14 minus a box equals 6, mixed in among ordinary ones. There is no working space and nothing to draw — the child reasons it out mentally and writes one number in the box.
G1-215.p2: This format quietly rewrites what the equals sign means. Most first graders read it as an instruction — now write the answer — and a page like this refuses to cooperate, because on many cards the answer is already printed. To fill the box the child has to see the sentence as a balance: something plus three is eight, so the something must be five. That shift is the beginning of algebraic thinking, and the classic error is beautifully diagnostic. A child who writes 11 where a box plus 3 equals 8 has added the two numbers they could see rather than read the sentence at all.
G1-215.p3: Print the PDF free and read the first equation aloud together, saying the box as the word something; that single habit clears up most of the confusion. Missing number equations to 10 offers a gentler version of exactly the same idea, and fact family houses to 20 shows why the flipped equations work.

G1-216.h1: Addition Facts to 20: Twelve Sums, No Subtraction
G1-216.title: Addition Facts to 20 for Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-216.metaDescription: Addition facts to 20 worksheet: twelve addition-only problems with an answer box each, solved mentally. Free printable Grade 1 PDF for fact fluency.
G1-216.p1: Every one of the twelve problems on this Grade 1 page is an addition, and all of them stay within 20. The sums are printed as bare facts in a grid, each ending in a box for the answer — nothing to count, nothing to color, and no subtraction slipped in to break the rhythm. Both addends are at least two, so there are no free plus-one facts padding the page. The child adds in their head and fills twelve boxes.
G1-216.p2: A single-operation page is worth having on the shelf even though mixed practice is the long-term goal. When every problem adds, the child can settle into one strategy and actually rehearse it — bridging through ten for 8 plus 5, leaning on a known double for 7 plus 6, counting on from the larger number for 9 plus 2 — instead of switching mental gears between one line and the next. That is how a strategy turns into a habit. Once it has, mixing the operations back in becomes the honest test of whether it really stuck.
G1-216.p3: The page prints free as a PDF and works well as the first half of a pair: run it one day and subtraction facts to 20 the next, so both directions get a clean session of their own. Fact families to 10 then shows the two operations as one relationship rather than two jobs.

G1-217.h1: Subtraction Facts to 20: A Whole Page of Take-Away
G1-217.title: Subtraction Facts to 20 for Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-217.metaDescription: Subtraction facts to 20 worksheet: twelve subtraction-only problems with an answer box each, solved in the head. Free printable Grade 1 PDF.
G1-217.p1: Twelve subtraction facts within 20 are laid out in a grid on this Grade 1 page, each with an answer box beside it. No additions appear anywhere, and there is no room for written working — the child reads a fact such as 15 minus 8, works it out mentally, and writes the difference. Both the number taken away and the answer are always at least two, so no card is solved for free.
G1-217.p2: Subtraction lags behind addition for most first graders, and a page devoted to it is the fastest way to find out why. There are two good routes to 15 minus 8 — counting back eight, or counting up from 8 to 15 — and they are not equally efficient. Children who only ever count back struggle badly once the gap grows, and they lose their place around ten. Watching which route a child takes on the harder facts tells you far more than the number of ticks does, and it points straight at the strategy that needs teaching next.
G1-217.p3: Print the PDF free and ask a child to explain one answer out loud, because that is where the strategy shows itself. Addition facts to 20 makes the natural companion sheet, and children who need the ideas underneath can spend a page on number bonds within 10 before coming back.

G1-218.title: Missing Number Equations to 10 | Free Printable PDF
G1-218.metaDescription: Missing number equations to 10 worksheet: twelve add and subtract problems with the box in a different place each time. Free printable Grade 1 PDF.
G1-218.p1: This Grade 1 page holds twelve equations that all stay within 10, and in each one an empty box stands where a number should be. Sometimes it sits at the end, sometimes at the front, sometimes in the middle: 4 plus a box equals 9, or a box minus 2 equals 5. Additions and subtractions are mixed together throughout. The child works out what belongs in the box mentally and writes it — one number per problem, twelve small pieces of detective work.
G1-218.p2: Small numbers make this a genuinely gentle introduction to a difficult idea. Missing-number work asks a child to think backwards, and if the arithmetic is demanding at the same time, the reasoning gets buried under the calculation. Within 10 the facts are usually already known, so all the effort lands where it belongs — on understanding what the sentence is actually asking. It also makes an unusually good partner activity: two children and one page produce far more talk than either would generate alone, because an empty box invites a guess and then a check.
G1-218.p3: The worksheet prints free as a PDF and slots neatly into small-group time. Children who find the boxes puzzling can meet the same idea drawn as a picture on number bonds within 10, and once the format feels familiar, missing number equations to 20 is the next rung on the ladder.

G1-219.h1: Fact Families to 10: Four Houses, Small Numbers
G1-219.title: Fact Families to 10 for Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-219.metaDescription: Fact families to 10 worksheet: four houses, each with three roof numbers and four related facts to complete. Free printable Grade 1 PDF for addition and subtraction.
G1-219.p1: Four fact family houses stand on this Grade 1 page. Three numbers sit on each triangular roof — a trio such as 3, 4 and 7 — and underneath them the four facts that trio makes are already printed: two additions and two subtractions, each ending in an empty box. The child reads the roof and completes all four, filling sixteen boxes across the page. Every number stays within 10, and no house uses a double.
G1-219.p2: Keeping the numbers small on a first fact family page is deliberate. The idea being taught here is structural — the same three numbers rearrange into four different sentences — and that idea is hard to notice if the child is busy working out whether 8 and 9 make 17. With every sum inside ten the arithmetic is nearly free, so the child's attention lands on the pattern instead: one trio, two orders for the addition, two starting points for the subtraction. Once a child has genuinely seen it, that pattern transfers to any numbers at all.
G1-219.p3: The page prints free as a PDF, and four houses make a comfortable first sitting. When the shape of the task is familiar, fact house practice to 10 offers more of the same easy numbers for fluency, and fact family houses to 20 raises the size of the trios.

G1-220.h1: Fact Family Houses to 20: Six Roofs to Fill
G1-220.title: Fact Family Houses to 20 | Free Printable PDF
G1-220.metaDescription: Fact family houses to 20 worksheet: six houses with teen trios on the roof and four related addition and subtraction facts each. Free printable Grade 1 PDF.
G1-220.p1: Six houses fill this Grade 1 page, and the trios on their roofs now reach into the teens — 9, 8 and 17, or 6, 14 and 20. Beneath each roof stand the four facts those three numbers make, two additions and two subtractions, every line ending in an empty box. Six houses means twenty-four answers on a single sheet, and the numbers are large enough that none of them can be guessed at a glance.
G1-220.p2: This is the progression page, and both of the things that changed matter. Larger numbers push the child past the facts they can simply see and into the teens, where addition and subtraction genuinely have to be worked out; six houses instead of four turns the exercise from a demonstration into practice with real volume behind it. That combination is what moves fact families from something we did in a lesson to a tool the child actually reaches for. It also rehearses crossing ten, over and over, inside a task that never once mentions it.
G1-220.p3: Print it free as a PDF. Children meeting the format for the first time will do better starting on fact families to 10, where the arithmetic stays out of the way, and once these six houses feel routine, mental math within 20 puts the very same facts to work without any scaffolding at all.

G1-221.h1: Fact House Practice to 10: Six Houses for Fluency
G1-221.title: Fact House Practice to 10 | Free Printable PDF
G1-221.metaDescription: Fact house practice worksheet: six fact family houses with trios within 10 and four related facts to complete in each. Free printable Grade 1 PDF.
G1-221.p1: Six fact family houses, every trio within 10, are printed on this Grade 1 page. Each roof carries three numbers, and each house holds the same four facts underneath — add them both ways, subtract them both ways — with an empty box at the end of every line. The format is the one children already know from earlier houses; what has changed is the quantity: six roofs, twenty-four boxes, and small friendly numbers the whole way down.
G1-221.p2: This one is built for the routine slot rather than the teaching slot. The concept has already been introduced, the numbers stay easy, and the point is repetition — the sort of page that works as morning work, as an early-finisher task, or in a folder a child can pick up without any instruction from an adult. Fluency in fact families is worth that kind of drip-feed: the children who write the four facts quickly and confidently are the ones who later meet 13 minus 5 and simply recall the addition that answers it.
G1-221.p3: The sheet prints free as a PDF, and running it a few times across a term costs nothing at all. Fact families to 10 is the shorter introduction if a child is meeting houses for the first time, while fact families with a missing partner takes the same easy trios and hides a different number instead.

G1-222.title: Fact Families: Missing Partner | Free Printable PDF
G1-222.metaDescription: Fact families missing partner worksheet: the result is printed and the middle number is blank in every fact. Four houses to complete. Free printable Grade 1 PDF.
G1-222.p1: Four houses stand on this Grade 1 page, and the facts underneath them have moved their gap. Each line reads something like 7 plus a box equals 12, or 12 minus a box equals 5: the result is printed at the end, and the number missing is the one in the middle. Using the three numbers on the roof, the child works out which partner belongs in each box — four facts per house, sixteen boxes in all, with every trio inside twenty.
G1-222.p2: Giving the child the roof and the results, but not the middle number, changes what the page actually tests. Instead of generating four facts from scratch, the child has to match: to look at 12 minus a box equals 5 and recognize which member of the trio is doing the work. That is much closer to how fact knowledge gets used in the wild, where a number is missing, the relationship is known, and the child reasons from what is in front of them. It also catches the child who has been copying roof numbers into the lines by position, without ever reading what the sentence says.
G1-222.p3: Print the PDF free and treat a wrong box as a conversation rather than a correction. Fact family houses to 20 is the version where the child produces every answer themselves, and missing number equations to 20 strips the houses away entirely and leaves the same reasoning standing bare.

G3-369.title: Multiply and Divide Fact Families | Free Printable PDF
G3-369.metaDescription: Multiplication and division fact families worksheet: four houses, each with a factor-factor-product roof and four related facts to complete. Free Grade 3 PDF.
G3-369.p1: Four houses fill this Grade 3 page, and the trios on their roofs are not addition families. Each roof carries a factor, a factor and their product — 6, 7 and 42, say — and underneath it the four related facts are printed with an empty box at the end of each: 6 × 7, 7 × 6, 42 ÷ 6 and 42 ÷ 7. Sixteen boxes, four families, factors between 2 and 9, and never the same factor twice in one house.
G3-369.p2: The house is familiar from first grade, and reusing it here is precisely the point: multiplication and division undo one another exactly as addition and subtraction do. What makes this version powerful is what it does to division. A child who reads 42 ÷ 6 as how many sixes fit inside forty-two is counting groups; a child who sees the house behind it thinks six times what makes forty-two, and simply recalls a fact they already own. That unknown-factor view is the single most useful idea in third-grade division, and it is worth far more than any division algorithm taught early.
G3-369.p3: The page prints free as a PDF and makes an excellent follow-up to table work, once the facts themselves are reasonably secure. The times table of 5 and the times table of 3 supply the raw recall these houses depend on, and fact families to 10 is where the same structure first appeared with plus and minus.

G1-223.h1: Number Words to 20: Circle the Matching Word
G1-223.title: Number Words to 20 for Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-223.metaDescription: Number words to 20 worksheet: six numerals, three written words beside each, circle the one that matches. Free printable Grade 1 PDF for reading numbers.
G1-223.p1: Six numerals between 3 and 20 are printed down this Grade 1 page, and beside each one stand three written number words on rounded chips. Only one of the three matches the numeral, and the near misses are close neighbors — a number one or two away, or ten apart — so a glance at the first letter is never enough. The child reads all three and circles the right one. Nothing has to be spelled or written: the whole task is reading, six times over.
G1-223.p2: The range matters more than it looks. Between three and twenty sit almost all of English's awkward number words: one, two and eight give the reader no help at all, eleven and twelve follow no pattern whatsoever, and thirteen and fifteen hide the roots they came from. These are words a child cannot decode their way into — they have to be known on sight, much the way sight words are — and a multiple-choice page is a low-stress way to build that recognition, because a near miss can be rejected without the child ever having to produce the correct spelling.
G1-223.p3: The sheet prints free as a PDF and takes about five minutes. Once these words are reliable, number words to 50 extends the range into the two-part compound numbers, and write the number words asks the child to produce the same words instead of picking them out of a line-up.

G1-224.h1: Tens in Words: Ten, Twenty, Thirty up to One Hundred
G1-224.title: Tens in Words: 10 to 100 | Free Printable PDF
G1-224.metaDescription: Tens in words worksheet: six round tens from 10 to 100, circle the matching written word. Fixes the forty-versus-fourteen mix-up. Free printable Grade 1 PDF.
G1-224.p1: This Grade 1 page keeps strictly to the round tens. Six numerals — 10, 20, 30 and their neighbors on up to 100 — are each printed with three written number words beside them, and the child circles the word that matches. Every numeral on the sheet is a multiple of ten, so the words in play are ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety and one hundred, and the wrong choices are drawn from the same family.
G1-224.p2: This is the page where the classic English confusion gets confronted head-on. For every ten from thirty to ninety, one of the two decoy words is its teen twin: forty against fourteen, sixty against sixteen, ninety against nineteen. The two families sound alike, look alike on the page, and mean wildly different amounts, and children who blur them make place-value errors that look like carelessness but are really vocabulary. Isolating the tens is what makes the difference audible — say the options out loud and the stressed ending gives the answer away. The odd spellings deserve a mention too, since forty loses the u that four keeps, and no rule explains it.
G1-224.p3: Print the PDF free and read the choices aloud as you go; the ear catches those endings faster than the eye ever will. Number words to 20 covers the teen half of the same confusion, and match numbers to number words puts both families side by side on one page.

G1-225.h1: Match Numbers to Number Words with a Line
G1-225.title: Match Numbers to Number Words | Free Printable PDF
G1-225.metaDescription: Matching worksheet for number words: five numerals in one column, five written words scrambled in the other, joined with a pencil line. Free printable Grade 1 PDF.
G1-225.p1: This Grade 1 page drops the multiple-choice format entirely. Five numerals stand in a column down the left, five written number words in a column down the right, and the child draws a line from each number to its word. The words are deliberately scrambled — no word sits opposite its own number — and the values run from the teens up toward one hundred, so the teen words and the tens words end up competing for the same lines.
G1-225.p2: Matching behaves differently from circling, and it is worth having both on hand. On a multiple-choice page every item is decided on its own; here the five pairs form one puzzle, so a wrong line makes a second one impossible, and children quickly discover the strategy of doing the certain ones first and reasoning out whatever is left. That process of elimination is genuine mathematical thinking rather than word recognition alone. It also means a single mistake becomes visible immediately — to the child as much as to the teacher — which makes the page unusually self-correcting.
G1-225.p3: Print the PDF free and encourage a light pencil line, because matching pages reward the child who is willing to change their mind. Number words to 20 and tens in words are the two pages that feed it, and write the number words is the harder step where nothing is offered to choose from.

G1-226.h1: Number Words to 50: Reading Two-Part Numbers
G1-226.title: Number Words to 50 for Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-226.metaDescription: Number words to 50 worksheet: six numerals from 13 to 50 with three written words each, circle the match. Compound hyphenated words. Free printable Grade 1 PDF.
G1-226.p1: The six numerals on this Grade 1 page run from 13 up to 50, each printed with three written number words for the child to choose between. What changes at this range is the shape of the words themselves: above twenty they arrive in two parts joined by a hyphen — twenty-six, thirty-one, forty-eight — so the child is now reading a small structure rather than recalling a single memorized word.
G1-226.p2: Two-part number words are where reading and place value meet. Twenty-six is not an arbitrary label; it says twenty and six, in that order, and a child who reads it that way is reading the number's structure straight off the page. The decoys on this sheet make that necessary, because one of them is often the same digits reversed — thirty-two lurking beside twenty-three — and options that share a first part or a second part cannot be told apart by glancing at the beginning. It is also the natural moment to mention the hyphen, which English uses on every compound number word from twenty-one to ninety-nine.
G1-226.p3: The page prints free as a PDF and makes a good five-minute station once the teen words are secure. Number words to 20 is the place to be solid before starting here, and tens in words handles the round numbers that form the first half of every compound word on this sheet.

G1-227.h1: Write the Number Words with a Word Bank
G1-227.title: Write the Number Words | Free Printable PDF
G1-227.metaDescription: Write the number words worksheet: a shuffled word bank at the top and six numerals, each above a writing line. Find the word and copy it. Free Grade 1 PDF.
G1-227.p1: A word bank runs across the top of this Grade 1 page, and beneath it six numerals wait, each printed above its own writing line. For every numeral the child finds the matching word in the bank and writes it out. The bank holds exactly the six words needed, shuffled out of order, and the numbers stay between 3 and 20 — words children already meet daily, except that this time nothing is circled and every letter has to be copied correctly.
G1-227.p2: Recognizing a word and producing it are two different skills, and the gap between them is where number-word work usually stalls. A child who circles fourteen without hesitation may still write it as forteen the moment the choice disappears. The word bank keeps this page honest rather than punishing: the correct spelling is right there to copy, so the child practises the act of writing the word — the letter order, the length, the look of the thing — with a model available. Because the bank holds six words for six numerals, it is also self-checking; a leftover word at the end means something above it went wrong.
G1-227.p3: Print the PDF free and expect it to take longer than the circling pages, since writing is slower and that is entirely fine. Number words to 20 is the recognition page that comes first, and match numbers to number words sits neatly between the two in difficulty.

G1-228.h1: Counting Coins: First Steps with Small Handfuls
G1-228.title: Counting Coins: First Steps | Free Printable PDF
G1-228.metaDescription: Beginner counting coins worksheet: four purses holding only two or three pennies, nickels and dimes. Write each total in cents. Free printable Grade 1 money PDF.
G1-228.p1: Four purses are printed on this Grade 1 page, and each one holds only two or three coins. The coins come from the three smallest kinds — pennies, nickels and dimes — so no quarter appears anywhere on the sheet. The child counts what is in each purse and writes the total in cents in the box beside it. Four purses, four totals, and never more than three coins to keep track of at a time.
G1-228.p2: A first money page should be about the coins themselves, not about the counting. Before a child can add money at all, they have to know that this small silver disc is worth five while the slightly smaller one beside it is worth ten — a genuinely strange idea, since size and value openly disagree, and one that plenty of first graders quietly get wrong for months. Holding each handful to three coins leaves attention free for exactly that recognition work, and the missing quarter is deliberate too, because twenty-five is the value that turns simple counting into a real chain.
G1-228.p3: Print the PDF free, and if you have real coins nearby, lay them straight onto the pictures as you go. Counting pennies and nickels narrows the job even further to two coin kinds, while counting money with all the coins brings the quarter in as soon as the child is ready for it.

G1-229.h1: Counting Money: All Four Coins in Every Purse
G1-229.title: Counting Money: All the Coins | Free Printable PDF
G1-229.metaDescription: Counting money worksheet with all four coins: six purses holding five to seven pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters. Write each total. Free printable Grade 1 PDF.
G1-229.p1: Six purses, five to seven coins in each, and every kind of coin in play — pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters can all turn up in the same handful on this Grade 1 page. The child works out the value of each purse and writes the total in cents in the box beside it. It is the fullest version of the coin-counting task and comfortably the busiest sheet in the money family.
G1-229.p2: With seven mixed coins in front of them, a child needs a method rather than good luck. The one worth teaching is order: sort the coins from the largest value down to the smallest, count the quarters first, then count on in tens, then fives, then ones. Children who instead work left to right across the picture lose their place constantly. The classic error also shows up here more than anywhere else — counting the number of coins rather than their values, so a purse holding six coins gets reported as six cents. Both habits are plainly visible in the answers.
G1-229.p3: The sheet prints free as a PDF and makes a fair end-of-unit check. Coin counting practice offers the same four coins in smaller handfuls for warming up first, and mental math within 20 sharpens the adding that every total on this page depends on.

G1-230.h1: Coin Counting Practice: Eight Purses on One Page
G1-230.title: Coin Counting Practice for Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-230.metaDescription: Coin counting practice worksheet: eight purses with three to five coins each, all four coin kinds. Write every total in cents. Free printable Grade 1 money PDF.
G1-230.p1: Eight purses are packed onto this Grade 1 page — the longest sheet in the money family — with three to five coins in each and all four coin kinds in circulation. For every purse the child adds up the values and writes the total in cents in the box. The handfuls themselves are moderate and no two purses hold the same combination; it is the sheer number of purses that turns this page into a workout.
G1-230.p2: Volume is the whole design here. Coin counting improves the way any counting skill improves — through repetition spread out over time rather than crammed into one lesson — and eight purses on a single page give a child enough repetitions in one sitting for the routine to start running by itself: recognize the coin, put the biggest first, count on. It also makes an honest progress check across a term. Run the same page in September and again in January and the difference in speed is obvious to the child, not only to the teacher.
G1-230.p3: Print it free as a PDF and use it more than once, since the coins are generated fresh every time you download the sheet. Counting money with all the coins is the harder cousin, with bigger handfuls and quarters throughout, and counting coins first steps is the gentle entry point if eight purses feels like a lot.

G1-231.h1: Counting Pennies and Nickels: Two-Coin Purses
G1-231.title: Counting Pennies and Nickels | Free Printable PDF
G1-231.metaDescription: Pennies and nickels worksheet: six purses holding two to four one-cent and five-cent coins. Count in fives, then ones. Free printable Grade 1 money PDF.
G1-231.p1: Only two kinds of coin appear on this Grade 1 page: pennies and nickels. Six purses each hold between two and four of them, and the child counts the value and writes the total in cents in the box beside it. With one-cent and five-cent coins alone, every total on the sheet stays small and every count follows the same simple two-step shape.
G1-231.p2: Restricting the coins isolates the strategy all money counting is built on: count the bigger coin first in fives, then add the ones on top. Five, ten, eleven, twelve — said out loud, that is exactly the rhythm the child will later use with dimes and quarters, and it is far easier to learn when only two values sit on the table. Pennies and nickels also make the value-versus-size lesson unmistakable, because the nickel is the fatter coin and worth five of the small ones. That contradiction is one children need to meet early, and often.
G1-231.p3: The page prints free as a PDF and suits a small group where the counting can be done aloud together. Counting coins first steps adds the dime to the mix, and once three coin kinds feel easy, counting money with all the coins brings in the quarter as well.

G1-232.h1: Which Purse Has More Money? Compare and Circle
G1-232.title: Which Purse Has More Money? | Free Printable PDF
G1-232.metaDescription: Comparing money worksheet: three rows of two purses, count both and circle the one worth more. Value versus number of coins. Free printable Grade 1 PDF.
G1-232.p1: This Grade 1 page shows three rows, and each row holds two purses side by side. The child counts the money in both, decides which one is worth more, and circles it — no totals have to be written down, though most children write them anyway. The two purses in a row never hold the same amount, and they rarely hold the same number of coins, which is exactly where the interest lies.
G1-232.p2: Comparing is where the biggest money misconception surfaces. Asked which is more, five pennies or one dime, a great many first graders confidently choose the five: more coins looks like more money, and nothing in their everyday counting has ever contradicted them. A page that deliberately sets a small pile of valuable coins against a large pile of cheap ones forces that question into the open. Once a child has been surprised by it two or three times, the idea that value and quantity are genuinely different things tends to stay put for good.
G1-232.p3: Print the PDF free and ask for the reason rather than just the circle, because how do you know is the whole lesson here. Coin counting practice builds the adding that this comparison rests on, and counting money with all the coins is the page to visit next once totals come quickly and reliably.
